back: Everything around the model: the loop, the tools, the permissions, the checks and the limits.
front: What is a harness?

back: The record of a run, in order: each model call, reply, permission, tool call and check.
front: What is a trace?

back: A trial is one run with one seed. A bench runs many trials of the same setup and reports the pass rate.
front: How is a trial different from a run?

back: It sets the random draws of a scripted run. The same seed gives the same run, so a bench repeats exactly.
front: What does a seed do?

back: The share of trials that pass their checks. It measures many runs, not one run.
front: What is a pass rate?

back: Verification and evals. A done claim stays a claim until a check runs and confirms it.
front: Which wire checks a done claim before the run is accepted?

back: Verification and evals. The harness took the model's word, so nothing checked the done claim.
front: The model says the tests pass, but no test ran. Which wire is that?

back: A named kind of failure that recurs across runs, such as a false done. Each module teaches one.
front: What is a failure family?

back: A model that reads a text and scores the possible next tokens. A harness calls it again and again.
front: What is a language model, in this course?

back: Every possible next token. Nothing in that step checks whether a token is true.
front: What does next-token prediction score?

back: It picks one token from the scored options, by the rules it is given. The model scores; the sampler picks.
front: What does sampling do?

back: It spreads the choice over more tokens, so less likely tokens get more chances. At zero, the top token always wins.
front: What does a higher temperature do to the choice?

back: A fluent, specific claim that is false. It reads the same as a true claim.
front: What is a hallucination?

back: Training sets the weights, before any chat. Inference reads them and leaves them the same.
front: What sets the weights, and what only reads them?

back: Verification. The harness took the reply's word, so nothing checked the claim.
front: A reply says all tests pass, and no test ran. Which wire is that?

back: No. Fluency shows how the reply reads. Only a check shows whether the claim is true.
front: Does a fluent reply show that it is true?

back: The part that cuts text into tokens. Real tokenizers differ, so a count from the course is an estimate.

back: About four characters per token. It is an estimate, and the Tokenizer labels it that way.
front: What is the course's rule of thumb for tokens?

back: No. A token can be a word, part of a word, or a punctuation mark.
front: Is a token always a word?

back: The fixed-size desk the model reads on each call. Instructions, earlier messages, tool results and the reply share it.
front: What is a context window?

back: Context. The desk is full, and the harness has no cap on what went onto it.
front: One tool result fills most of the window, so the next prompt cannot be sent. Which wire is that?

back: The most tokens one reply may use. A reply that reaches it stops there.
front: What is the output limit?

back: Input tokens are what the model reads on a call. Output tokens are what it writes. Both use the window.

back: More tokens in and out. Each token is work for the model, and prices are set per million tokens.
front: What makes a call slower and more costly?

back: The call starts from what it is sent, and nothing else. The model keeps nothing between calls.
front: What does stateless mean for a model call?

back: The ordered list of messages sent with each call. It is the conversation the model can see.
front: What is the messages array?

back: Whether it is from the user or from the assistant.
front: What does a role tell you about a message?

back: The earlier messages in the list. The harness keeps them and decides how much each call sends.
front: What is conversation history?

back: In the system prompt, kept apart from the messages. The harness sends it with every call.

back: Context and memory. It decides what stays in the window and what the model sees on each call.
front: Which wire decides what the next call sends from the history?

back: What is in the window and what is in saved files. The model's weights are not the harness's to change.
front: Which kind of memory does the harness control?

back: What the harness sends for one model call: the system prompt, the tools and the messages.
front: What is a request?

back: One typed part of a response: text, or a tool request. Its type says what fields it has.
front: What is a content block?

back: Why the model stopped: end_turn, tool_use, max_tokens and a few others. The harness acts on each one.
front: What does stop_reason tell the harness?

back: The response hit the request's length limit, so it may be cut off. Do not run a half-written tool request.
front: What is max_tokens as a stop reason?

back: The counts in a response: the input and output tokens of the call. The cost of a call comes from them.
front: What is usage?

back: A reply that arrives as a sequence of events. The events build the same message, in order.
front: What is streaming?

back: Because a reply can mix text and tool requests. Each block says which it is, so the harness reads them one by one.
front: Why is a reply a list of typed blocks, not one string?

back: A way to write down the shape of a JSON object: its fields, their types, which are required and which values are allowed.
front: What is JSON Schema?

back: It refuses a field the schema does not name. This course's checker refuses it.
front: What does additionalProperties false do?

back: A field that may take only one of a short list of values.
front: What is an enum?

back: Checking a value against a schema before the harness uses it. It returns the first reason the value fails.
front: What is schema validation?

back: A reply in a shape you asked for. The shape can be right and the values still wrong.
front: What is a structured output?

back: Tools. The check is on the call's input, before the tool runs.

back: Generating a reply so that only the tokens a schema allows can be chosen. A method, compared with the other two.
front: What is constrained decoding?

back: Extra tokens the model writes before it answers, to work a problem out. They are billed as output.
front: What is extended thinking?

back: It goes back to the model complete and unmodified, with the tool call that it belongs to.
front: What must happen to a thinking block during a tool loop?

back: A setting that tells the model how much to work before it answers. The harness sets it on each request.
front: What is effort?

back: The cost of a task's calls, divided by the share of tasks that finish. A cheap call that often fails is not cheap.
front: What is cost per completed task?

back: Control. The harness decides how much the model works before it answers.
front: The board sets effort to low for every call. Which wire is that setting on?

back: No. On easy work it can add cost and wait without a better answer.
front: Does a higher effort always help?

back: A model saying its work is good when it is not. Checking its own work does not catch it.
front: What is self-praise, as a failure mode?

back: A check that does not depend on the model's words: a test, a file, a number you can look up.
front: What is ground truth?

back: When each step can fail, the chance that all the steps work falls with every step.
front: What is a compounding error?

back: From the system around the model, checked from outside the model.
front: Where does reliability come from in this course?

back: Facts the model holds that have changed since it learned them. The model does not know they are out of date.
front: What is stale knowledge?

back: Verification and evals. The check is outside the model's words.
front: A check that runs the tests after the model says done. Which wire is it?

back: The model can give different answers to the same prompt, so one good run says little about the next.
front: What is randomness, as a failure mode?

back: It writes a tool_use block that names the tool and its input. It does not run the tool. The harness does.
front: What does the model do when it wants a tool run?

back: tool_use. The harness runs the tools, then calls the model again with the results.
front: What stop reason tells the harness that a tool run is needed?

back: A name, a description and an input schema.
front: What three parts make a tool definition?

back: The fields the tool takes, their types, and which of them are required.
front: What does input_schema say?

back: The tool_use_id of the call it answers.
front: What must each tool_result carry?

back: Set is_error to true and say why in the content.
front: How do you mark a failed call?

back: All together in one user message, sent after the reply.
front: Where do the results of one reply go?

back: The model sees only the definition. The name, the description and the schema are its whole picture of the tool, so a poor definition leads to misuse.
front: Why is a tool a user interface for a model?

back: One call to the model, plus the tool results that follow it.

front: What is a turn limit?

back: A cap on the total tokens a run may use, input and output together. The loop checks it before each call.
front: What is a token budget?

back: The model's own statement that it finished, carried by end_turn. The loop checks it. It is not proof.

back: Loop & state. Every run needs more than one exit.
front: Which wire asks: what happens next, what do we carry, and when do we stop?

back: Verification & evals. A done claim stays a claim until a check confirms it.
front: Which wire checks the model's done claim before the loop accepts it?

back: The two results for one reply sit in two user messages. Send all of them together, in one user message.
front: Spot the bug in this history.

back: Choosing the words of the prompt and the instructions. Words guide the model; they do not enforce anything.

back: The harness you add around a model product or API: your loop, your tools and your checks.
front: What is a user harness?

back: A process runs the same steps each time. A model writes different text each run, so the harness must check its output.

back: A library of ready-made parts for building a harness. It does not decide your harness for you.

back: One turn of a run as eight wires in order, with the harness settings beside them.

back: If it isn't in the trace, it didn't happen.

back: A tool is a user interface for a model.
front: Which law goes with Tools?

back: Verification & evals. Nothing checked the done claim.
front: The model says the tests pass, and nothing ran them. Which wire is at fault?

back: One block of text in the prompt that tells the model what to do: the system prompt, the project rules, the user's message or a tool result.

back: The instruction hierarchy: who wrote each layer, not what it says. A tool result is data, not an instruction.
front: What decides which layer wins when two disagree?

back: How specific it is. Too low and it is a lookup table; too high and it is a slogan.
front: What is altitude in an instruction?

back: Code that runs before each tool call and decides whether it may run. It holds whatever the prompt says.

back: When the check cannot decide, it denies the action. A hook that fails open lets the action through when it breaks.
front: What does fail closed mean for a hook?

back: Where things live, the commands that check them, and the rules that must hold. Not every case, and not a manual.

front: The project rules say never touch tests/, and only the prompt holds it. Which wire is that?

back: The fall in answer quality as the window fills, well before the hard limit.

back: Each part of the context in tokens: instructions, tool definitions, history and tool outputs.

back: Don't load it, shrink it, move it out, summarize it.
front: What are the four levers, in order?

back: The start and the end of the output, and how many characters were cut, so the reader can ask for a smaller range.
front: What does an output cap keep, and what does it say?

back: Stable material first, the current task last.
front: How should context be ordered for attention?

back: Context. The desk is full, and nothing caps what went onto it.
front: One tool output fills most of the window, so the next prompt cannot be sent. Which wire is that?

back: No. Quality can fall well before the window is full.
front: Does a window that fits mean the model reads all of it equally well?

back: Replacing the older messages with a summary, so the desk has room. The summary keeps only what the harness chose to keep.
front: What is compaction?

back: It loses what matters: a constraint or a decision that the summary did not keep is gone for every later call.
front: What is the main failure of compaction?

back: Raw tool output. It keeps the goal, the constraints, the decisions, the progress and the file pointers.
front: What should a compactor drop?

back: When the run has drifted and the goal is clearer as a fresh start. Compaction suits a clear thread that only needs room.

back: The window, the session log, the project files and the long-term store.

back: Context. The desk lost the commitment, and the compactor's keep list decided what stayed.

back: The part of a request before a point. The cache matches a whole prefix or none of it.
front: What is a cache prefix?

back: Stable first, changing last: the tools, then the system prompt, then the messages, with the new message at the end.
front: Put the parts of a request in the order the cache reads them.

back: A change that makes earlier cache entries stop matching. The next call writes the request again.
front: What is cache invalidation?

back: A read takes input from the cache at a low price. A write stores input in the cache at a higher price, once.
front: What is a cache read, compared with a cache write?

back: The share of the input that was read from the cache. Compute it from the read tokens over all the input tokens.
front: What is a cache hit rate?

back: The point up to which a request asks to be cached. The course's model uses one, at the end of the request.
front: What is a cache breakpoint?

back: A block that changes on every call, such as a clock line. Wherever it sits, the blocks after it miss.
front: Which block breaks a cache when it changes on every call?

back: How long a cache entry lasts after it was last written or read. The default is five minutes.
front: What is a cache TTL?

back: Everything the run remembers between calls: messages, turn count and status. It lives in one place, and one function changes it.
front: What is run state?

back: The one word that says how the run ended. A run has one final status, set by one exit.
front: What is a final status?

back: A tool call with no result after it. The next request holding it is refused, so the harness must answer it.
front: What is an orphaned tool call?

back: Everything the run needs to start again: the messages, the turn count and the pending calls, saved together.
front: What does pause and resume need from the state?

back: A history that only grows at the end. A resumed run keeps the same earlier messages.
front: What is append-only history?

back: Noticing the same action repeated across the last few calls, and stopping the run before the turn limit.
front: What is loop detection?

back: A stop that a person asks for during a run. The harness answers the pending calls, then ends or resumes the run.
front: What is an interrupt?

back: A failure likely to pass on its own. A retry may succeed, so the harness retries it with a limit.
front: What is a transient error?

back: A failure that repeats on every try. The harness does not retry it: it fixes the request, or stops.
front: What is a permanent error?

back: A wait that doubles after each failed try, up to a cap.
front: What is exponential backoff?

back: Clients that failed together would retry together. A random part of the wait spreads their retries out.
front: Why does jitter matter?

back: After a set number of failures in a row, it opens and holds calls back for a cooldown, so retries stop adding load.
front: What does a circuit breaker do?

back: A limit on the retries a run or client may make, so retries cannot grow without end.
front: What is a retry budget?

back: A value sent with a request, so a repeated request is recognised and not run twice.
front: What is an idempotency key?

back: The tools as the model sees them: names, descriptions, inputs and results. Design it for the model, as you would a screen for a person.
front: What is an agent-computer interface?

back: It tells the model what the tool does and when to use it. The model reads it on every call, so vague words cost calls.
front: What is a tool description for?

back: It names what went wrong and what to do next, in a few words. A bare 'Invalid input' leaves the model guessing.
front: What makes an error actionable?

back: A tool that does not change its environment. A read-only hint says so, and a hint is not a check.
front: What is a read-only tool?

back: A tool that may change or delete things. Treat its call as a decision, not a read.
front: What is a destructive tool?

back: When neither writes a resource the other reads or writes. A read and an edit of the same file are not.
front: When are two tool calls parallel-safe?

back: The tools wire: the definitions are sent with every call.
front: On which wire does a tool description sit?

back: A hint a tool server gives about a tool. Clients should not make tool-use decisions on untrusted annotations.

back: Tools, resources and prompts. The client reaches them through a transport.

back: How messages move between a client and a server. Stdio sends newline-delimited messages over a subprocess's standard streams.
front: What is a transport?

back: The name and description load first. The full procedure loads only when the task needs it.
front: What is progressive disclosure for a skill?

back: YAML frontmatter, then the procedure in Markdown. The frontmatter carries the name and the description.
front: What is a SKILL.md file?

back: Finding a tool's definition by keyword and loading it for the next call, instead of sending every definition each time.
front: What is tool search?

back: Tokens on every call, and a harder choice for the model. Measure both before you add a tool.
front: What does a long list of tool definitions cost?

back: Many round trips, each with its own result, with one program that calls several tools and returns one result.
front: What does programmatic tool calling replace?

back: As untrusted hints. Do not make a permission decision on them alone.

back: As action times target. The same command can be safe in one place and dangerous in another.
front: How is risk judged?

back: Test it with a table of cases, each with the decision it must give.

back: Permissions. A decision in code holds; a line in the prompt only asks.

back: Allow them, so that the prompts left are the ones that matter.

back: How bad a mistake can get, whatever the permissions said.

back: It normalizes the path, then refuses it if it lands outside the workspace root.
